title: The Periodic Table: Groups and Trends
description: Use proton number, periods and groups to predict properties; compare alkali metals, halogens, transition elements and noble gases, including displacement reactions and group trends for Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: How the Table Is Organised
notes.body:
📌 The Periodic Table arranges elements in order of increasing **proton number**. Horizontal rows are **periods**; vertical columns are **groups**.

🔑 Position predicts structure and chemistry
• Period number = number of occupied electron shells.
• For Groups I–VII, group number = number of outer-shell electrons.
• Group I and II metals commonly form 1+ and 2+ ions; Group VI and VII non-metals commonly form 2− and 1− ions.
• Elements in a group react similarly because their atoms have the same number of outer-shell electrons.

💡 Worked Example
An atom with configuration 2,8,7 is in Period 3 and Group VII. It gains one electron to form a 1− ion.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Ordering the table by mass number. The organising quantity is proton number, not relative atomic mass.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Read period from shells, group from outer electrons, and likely ion charge from the group.

notes.heading: Across a Period: Metal to Non-metal
notes.body:
📌 Moving left to right across Period 3, elements change from metallic to non-metallic character. The Periodic Table therefore lets you predict bonding, oxide behaviour and physical properties from position.

🔑 Using unfamiliar information
Do not memorise a property for every element. Compare its position with a nearby known element and use supplied data to identify a trend. Group trends are especially useful when a question gives melting points, densities or reaction observations for several members.

💡 Worked Example
An element in Group II is expected to be a metal, lose two electrons and form an ion with charge 2+. A Group VII element is expected to be a non-metal and form a 1− ion or share one electron.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming every property changes in the same direction. Metallic character decreases across a period, but individual physical properties must be inferred from the data given.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Position gives a prediction; numerical trends must be supported by the information in the question.

notes.heading: Group I: The Alkali Metals
notes.body:
📌 Lithium, sodium and potassium are relatively soft metals with low densities. They react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

🔑 Trends down Group I
• Melting point **decreases**.
• Density **increases**.
• Reactivity **increases**: lithium reacts least vigorously of the three and potassium most vigorously.

💡 Worked Example
Predict rubidium, below potassium, to be softer-looking and more reactive with water than potassium, with a lower melting point and higher density. Only make predictions within the stated trends.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reversing the trends or describing these metals as hard and unreactive. Their outer electron is lost increasingly easily down the group in the exam explanation.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Down Group I: melting point down; density and reactivity up. Always include the correct hydroxide and hydrogen products for water reactions.

illustration.alt: Two group columns show alkali metal reactivity increasing down Group I and halogen reactivity decreasing down Group VII, with melting point decreasing for Group I and density increasing for both groups.
illustration.caption: Group I and Group VII have opposite reactivity trends; use the direction shown rather than guessing from a single property.

notes.heading: Group VII: The Halogens
notes.body:
📌 Chlorine, bromine and iodine are diatomic non-metals: Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. At room temperature and pressure, chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid.

🔑 Trends down Group VII
• Density **increases**.
• Reactivity **decreases**.
• The appearances also become darker, useful when interpreting an unfamiliar halogen.

💡 Worked Example
Astatine is below iodine, so predict a darker solid with greater density and lower reactivity than iodine. Do not infer an exact melting point without data.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying the Group I reactivity trend to halogens. The two groups show opposite trends: Group I becomes more reactive down the group; Group VII becomes less reactive.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Know the three appearances and formulas as well as the two required trends.

notes.heading: Halogen Displacement
notes.body:
📌 A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

🔑 The rule
chlorine displaces bromine and iodine; bromine displaces iodine but not chlorine; iodine displaces neither.

💡 Worked Example
Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq). A red-brown colour appears because bromine forms. With potassium chloride and bromine there is no reaction: bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine.

🔑 Ionic view
For chlorine with bromide ions: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Potassium ions are spectators.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a reaction simply because two chemicals were mixed. First compare reactivity; no displacement is a valid answer.

📎 Key Points to Remember
The halogen higher in Group VII wins. Link any colour observation to the halogen produced.

notes.heading: Transition Elements
notes.body:
📌 Transition elements are metals with high densities and high melting points. They form coloured compounds and often act as catalysts, either as elements or in compounds.

🔑 Extended feature
They have ions with variable oxidation numbers. Iron commonly forms iron(II), Fe²⁺, and iron(III), Fe³⁺, compounds. The Roman numeral names the oxidation number and prevents confusion between different compounds.

💡 Worked Example
FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride and FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride. The charges balance because chloride is Cl⁻ in both compounds.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying Group I trends to transition metals or saying all metal compounds are coloured. Coloured compounds and variable oxidation numbers are characteristic of transition elements, not every metal.

📎 Key Points to Remember
High density, high melting point, coloured compounds, catalysis and variable oxidation numbers.

notes.heading: Group VIII: Noble Gases
notes.body:
📌 Noble gases are unreactive, monatomic gases. Monatomic means their particles are single atoms, not molecules such as O₂ or Cl₂.

🔑 Why they are unreactive
They have full outer electron shells: helium has 2 electrons; the other noble gases have 8 outer electrons. They do not normally need to gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable configuration.

💡 Worked Example
Argon has configuration 2,8,8. Three occupied shells place it in Period 3, and its full outer shell places it in Group VIII.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling helium's outer shell incomplete because it contains 2 rather than 8. The first shell is full with 2 electrons.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Full outer shell → very low reactivity; monatomic → individual atoms. Use both ideas in an explanation.

flashcards.definition: Elements are arranged in periods and groups in order of increasing proton number.
flashcards.example: An atom with 12 protons is magnesium regardless of its isotope mass.

flashcards.definition: Elements in a group have similar chemical properties because their atoms have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
flashcards.example: Sodium and potassium both have one outer electron and form 1+ ions.

flashcards.definition: Elements change from metallic to non-metallic character from left to right.
flashcards.example: Period 3 begins with metals such as sodium and ends with non-metals such as chlorine and argon.

flashcards.definition: Down the group, melting point decreases while density and reactivity increase.
flashcards.example: Potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium.

flashcards.definition: A metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas form; reactivity increases down Group I.
Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid at r.t.p.
flashcards.example: Bromine is the only one of the three that is liquid at r.t.p.

flashcards.definition: Down the group, density increases and reactivity decreases; all named halogens are diatomic.
flashcards.example: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine.

flashcards.definition: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its halide solution.
flashcards.example: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂; bromine does not displace chlorine.

flashcards.definition: Dense, high-melting metals that form coloured compounds and often act as catalysts.
flashcards.example: Transition-metal compounds are used as catalysts in industrial processes.

flashcards.definition: Transition elements can form ions with different charges or oxidation numbers.
flashcards.example: Iron forms Fe²⁺ in iron(II) chloride and Fe³⁺ in iron(III) chloride.

flashcards.definition: Unreactive monatomic gases whose atoms have full outer electron shells.
flashcards.example: Argon exists as single Ar atoms with configuration 2,8,8.

flashcards.definition: The first electron shell is complete with two electrons, so helium is a noble gas.

questions.stem: In what order are elements arranged in the modern Periodic Table?
questions.explanation: The Periodic Table is arranged by increasing proton number, also called atomic number. Nucleon number can differ between isotopes of the same element.

questions.stem: Why do sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties?
choices: They have the same number of electron shells
Their atoms each have one outer-shell electron
questions.explanation: Both are in Group I, so each atom has one outer-shell electron. Similar outer electronic configurations produce similar chemistry.

questions.stem: Which description of bromine at room temperature and pressure is correct?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Chlorine is the pale yellow-green gas and iodine is the grey-black solid.

questions.stem: Which statement about noble gases is correct?
choices: They are monatomic and have full outer electron shells
They are diatomic and highly reactive
They all have exactly eight electrons in total
questions.explanation: Noble gases exist as single atoms and are unreactive because their outer shells are full. Helium has only two electrons in total, filling its first shell.

questions.stem: An atom has electronic configuration 2,8,6. Which ion is it most likely to form?
questions.explanation: The atom is in Group VI with six outer electrons. It gains two electrons to complete its outer shell, forming a 2− ion.

questions.stem: Which row gives the trends down Group I?
choices: Melting point decreases; density increases; reactivity increases
Melting point increases; density decreases; reactivity decreases
Melting point decreases; density decreases; reactivity increases
Melting point increases; density increases; reactivity increases
questions.explanation: Down Group I, melting point decreases while density and reactivity increase. Potassium is therefore more reactive than lithium and sodium.

questions.stem: Chlorine is bubbled through aqueous potassium bromide. What happens?
choices: No reaction because both contain Group VII elements
Chlorine displaces bromine and a red-brown colour appears
Bromine displaces chlorine and a pale green colour disappears
questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. The bromine produced gives a red-brown colour.

questions.stem: Which property is characteristic of transition elements but not Group I metals?
choices: They form coloured compounds and can have variable oxidation numbers
They are solids at room temperature
questions.explanation: Transition elements form coloured compounds and have variable oxidation numbers, such as Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. These are not defining Group I properties.

questions.stem: Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous potassium iodide. Which ionic equation represents the reaction?
questions.explanation: Bromine is more reactive than iodine and displaces it. Potassium ions are spectators, so they do not appear in the ionic equation.

questions.stem: Element X is below iodine in Group VII. Which prediction is most reasonable?
choices: X is less dense and more reactive than iodine
X is a pale yellow-green gas
X is more dense and less reactive than iodine
X is a soft metal that forms X⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Density increases and reactivity decreases down Group VII. X is therefore predicted to be denser and less reactive than iodine; exact appearance requires further information.

questions.stem: A solution contains chloride, bromide and iodide ions. Chlorine is added. Which ions are oxidised?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than both bromine and iodine, so it removes electrons from Br⁻ and I⁻, forming Br₂ and I₂. It cannot displace itself from chloride.

questions.stem: Which particle has a full outer shell but is NOT monatomic?
questions.explanation: Cl₂ contains two chlorine atoms covalently bonded, each with a complete outer shell, so it is diatomic. He, Ne and Ar are monatomic noble gases.

questions.stem: Which change occurs from left to right across Period 3?
choices: The number of occupied shells increases
Every element becomes a better electrical conductor
questions.explanation: Across a period the elements change from metallic to non-metallic character. Proton number increases while the number of occupied shells stays constant.

questions.stem: Rubidium is below potassium in Group I. Which reaction should be most vigorous with cold water?
questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down Group I. Rubidium is lowest of the four elements listed, so it is predicted to react most vigorously.

questions.stem: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Which displacement reaction is predicted to occur?
choices: Astatine displaces iodine from potassium iodide
Iodine displaces astatine from sodium astatide
Chlorine cannot displace astatine from sodium astatide
Astatine displaces chlorine from sodium chloride
questions.explanation: Iodine is above astatine and therefore more reactive, so it displaces astatine from an astatide solution. Chlorine, being still higher, can also displace astatine.
